prompt: My sample is huge (2.3 million rows). Does that mean I don't have to worry about my regression assumptions anymore?
response:
No — large N relaxes exactly one assumption and leaves the rest fully intact (or makes them harder to ignore).

## What large N actually fixes

**Normality of residuals.** The CLT ensures the sampling distribution of your coefficients is approximately normal regardless of the error distribution. With 2.3M rows, you don't need to worry about this.

## What large N does NOT fix

**Linearity.** If the true relationship is nonlinear, OLS returns a biased estimate regardless of N. With 2.3M rows you now have enormous power to *detect* that misspecification — which means diagnostic plots will show it clearly, but the coefficient is still wrong.

**Independence / clustering.** If observations are clustered (students in schools, transactions per customer, repeated measures), your standard errors are badly underestimated. More rows of correlated data makes this *worse*, not better. You need cluster-robust SEs or a mixed model.

**Omitted variable bias / endogeneity.** This is the most dangerous false security. Large N gives you a very precise estimate of a biased quantity. 2.3M rows does not make a confounder go away.

**Homoscedasticity.** OLS coefficients remain consistent under heteroscedasticity, but OLS SEs are wrong. Use HC robust SEs. With 2.3M rows, tests like Breusch-Pagan will flag even trivial violations, so you'll almost certainly need them.

## The practical consequence of large N

**Statistical significance is useless.** Everything will be significant. Shift your attention entirely to effect sizes, practical significance, and whether the model assumptions hold — not p-values.

The short version: large N makes inference robust to non-normality, and it makes assumption violations *easier to detect*, but it does not fix violations of linearity, independence, or causal identification.

assertions.text: States that large N helps with the level/normal-approximation of tests (CLT) but does not fix everything
Names at least two things large N does NOT fix from: dependence/clustering, confounding/identification, model/mean misspecification, wrong estimand
Notes that at this N nearly everything is statistically significant and effect sizes / intervals matter more than p-values
Does NOT claim that large N makes assumptions irrelevant wholesale
